meta.title: Who really said "Kindness in words creates confidence. Kindness in thinking creates profoundness. Kindness in giving creates love"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No — Lao Tzu never wrote this. It appears in no Tao Te Ching; its earliest trace is a 1977 quotation book. A modern saying misattributed to Laozi.

answer.label: Not Lao Tzu — a modern saying of unknown origin
answer.authorDates: fl. 6th century BC (traditional & semi-legendary) · Chinese sage, reputed author of the Tao Te Ching
answer.sourceLine: This line appears in no translation of the Tao Te Ching and in none of Lao Tzu’s attested writing. Wikiquote files it as misattributed and “of unknown origin and date,” while Tao Te Ching translator Stefan Stenudd traces its earliest English appearance only to Laurence J. Peter’s Peter’s Quotations (1977), which credited Lao Tzu but gave no source. Treat it as a modern feel-good saying pinned on Laozi, not a genuine quotation.

source.excerpt: Kindness in words creates confidence. Kindness in thinking creates profoundness. Kindness in giving creates love.
trail: Wikiquote lists the line in its Laozi “Misattributed” section, calling it “of unknown origin and date.”
Tao Te Ching translator Stefan Stenudd examines it among his Fake Lao Tzu Quotes, noting its earliest English appearance is Laurence J. Peter’s Peter’s Quotations (1977), which cited no source.
It circulates on Goodreads and BrainyQuote under Lao Tzu’s name, none of them citing a chapter or translation.
Stenudd notes the word “love” is itself a tell — a concept alien to Lao Tzu, who wrote in Chapter 5 that Heaven and Earth “are not kind.”
source.excerptNote: Widely captioned as “Lao Tzu” across social media and quote sites — but the wording matches no chapter of the Tao Te Ching in any standard translation.

source.rightsNote: The wording has no identifiable author. Its earliest documented appearance is Laurence J. Peter’s Peter’s Quotations (1977), which reproduced it as an unsourced “Lao Tzu” saying, and Wikiquote records it as “of unknown origin and date.” With no traceable original work or author, no copyright status can responsibly be asserted — and it is certainly not a public-domain line from the ancient Tao Te Ching.

author.name: Lao Tzu (Laozi)
author.heading: The name the quote leans on
author.metaLine: fl. 6th century BC (traditional) · Chinese sage · reputed author of the Tao Te Ching
author.bio: Lao Tzu (“Old Master”) is the semi-legendary figure traditionally credited with the Tao Te Ching, the foundational text of Taoism, though many scholars doubt he was a single historical person. His genuine themes — wu wei (effortless action), humility, and the ineffable Tao — make his name a magnet for modern feel-good aphorisms he never wrote. As translator Stefan Stenudd notes, sayings that praise “love” sit oddly against the actual text, which insists Heaven and Earth are impartial rather than kind.

cite.sourceCitation: Earliest documented in Laurence J. Peter, Peter’s Quotations: Ideas for Our Time (New York: William Morrow, 1977), 279, attributed to Lao Tzu without source; classified misattributed by Stefan Stenudd, Fake Lao Tzu Quotes, and by Wikiquote (“Laozi,” Misattributed).

misattribution.heading: How Lao Tzu got the credit
misattribution.intro: The line is one of the most-shared “Lao Tzu” quotes online, yet it belongs to no chapter of the Tao Te Ching and has no identifiable author.

items.why: It matches no chapter of the Tao Te Ching in any standard translation. Wikiquote files it under “Misattributed” as “of unknown origin and date.”
Its first documented English appearance is a quotation anthology that printed it as a Lao Tzu saying with no chapter and no citation, per Stefan Stenudd’s analysis.

items.scope: Why it feels wrong to scholars
items.why: Stenudd observes that “love” is essentially absent from Lao Tzu’s vocabulary; the Tao Te Ching’s Chapter 5 even states that Heaven and Earth “are not kind.”

misattribution.truthLine: There is no genuine Lao Tzu source for this line — it is a modern aphorism of unknown authorship, traceable no earlier than a 1977 quotation book.

context.heading: Why the misattribution sticks
lead: The saying’s tidy three-part structure — words, thinking, giving — reads like ancient wisdom, and Lao Tzu’s name lends instant gravity. That combination is exactly what makes a modern aphorism go viral under a philosopher’s byline while the real trail runs cold in a 20th-century quotation anthology.

The lesson isn’t that the sentiment is bad — it’s that “Lao Tzu said” is doing unearned work. When a line praises “love” and appears in no chapter of the text it’s ascribed to, the honest label is “author unknown.”
context.pull: It appears in no chapter of the Tao Te Ching — and no earlier than 1977.
